{{ElectionsOH}}
The '''2006 United States Senate election in Ohio''' was held on November 7, 2006. Incumbent Republican [[Mike DeWine]] ran for re-election, but was defeated by Democratic Congressman [[Sherrod Brown]].<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/democrats-score-first-senate-win/ | work=CBS News | title=Democrats Score First Senate Win | date=November 7, 2006 | access-date=November 8, 2006 | archive-date=May 24, 2011 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110524014608/http://www.cbsnews.com/stories/2006/11/07/politics/main2161152.shtml | url-status=live }}</ref> As of {{YEAR}}, this is the most recent time a Democratic Senate candidate in Ohio won a race by double digits. This was also the last time an incumbent senator lost reelection in Ohio, until Brown was defeated in [[2024 United States Senate election in Ohio|2024]] by [[Bernie Moreno]].

To date, this is [[Mike DeWine |Mike DeWine's]] second general election loss of his political career, following his 1992 loss to John Glenn. Following his defeat, DeWine served as Ohio's state attorney general from 2011 to 2019, and has been the state's governor since 2019.

== Background ==
The [[incumbent]] [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Senator [[Mike DeWine|R. Michael DeWine]] had approval ratings at 38%,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://surveyusa.com/50State2006/100USSenatorApproval061024Net.htm |title=www.surveyusa.com. |access-date=October 28, 2006 |archive-date=December 1, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161201050516/http://www.surveyusa.com/50State2006/100USSenatorApproval061024Net.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> making him the second most unpopular U.S. senator behind [[Pennsylvania]] Republican [[Rick Santorum]], who was also up for reelection in 2006. Pre-election stories in the U.S. media suggested that the national Republican Party might have given up on saving Senator DeWine's Senate seat before election day.{{Citation needed|date=February 2021}} [[Sherrod Brown]], former [[Ohio secretary of state]] and U.S. representative from [[United States House of Representatives, Ohio District 13|Ohio's 13th district]], easily won the Democratic nomination over [[Merrill Keiser|Merrill Keiser Jr]].

== Republican primary ==
=== Candidates ===
* [[Mike DeWine]], incumbent U.S. senator since 1995
* William G. Pierce, engineer
* David Smith, candidate for U.S. representative from Ohio's 2nd congressional district in [[Ohio's 2nd congressional district special election, 2005|2005]]

=== Campaign ===
Both candidates campaigned as conservative alternatives to DeWine, citing DeWine's support for gun control measures and his role as a member of the [[Gang of 14]], a group of Republicans who compromised with Democrats in a dispute about judicial appointments.

== General election ==

=== Candidates ===
* [[Sherrod Brown]], U.S. representative from [[Lorain, Ohio|Lorain]] (Democratic)
* [[Mike DeWine]], incumbent senator since 1995 (Republican)
* Richard Duncan (Independent) (write-in)

=== Campaign ===
The Republican Party, which was facing multiple challenges to their Senate majority, was initially determined to assist DeWine in his competitive race, while the National Democratic party supported Brown in hopes of taking control of the Senate. John McClelland, a spokesman for the Ohio Republican Party, said, "It's vitally important to the Republican Party as a whole, so I think that's why you see the president coming to Ohio to support Mike DeWine." Phil Singer, a spokesman for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, said, "Mike DeWine Senior is in for the fight of his life, make no mistake about it."<ref name="KyPost Collins">{{cite news | title=Bush visit all politics this time | first=Michael | last=Collins | work=[[The Cincinnati Post|The Kentucky Post]] | location=[[Covington, Kentucky]] | publisher=[[E. W. Scripps Company]] | date=February 23, 2006 | url=http://news.cincypost.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=2006602230383 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060828020907/http://news.cincypost.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=2006602230383 | archive-date=August 28, 2006}}</ref>

On July 14, 2006, DeWine's campaign began airing TV commercials depicting a smoking [[World Trade Center (1973–2001)|World Trade Center]]. "The senator was notified... by a reporter at ''[[U.S. News & World Report]]'' that the image of the burning Twin Towers could not have depicted the actual event because the smoke was blowing the wrong way."<ref name=autogenerated1>[https://www.usnews.com/usnews/news/articles/060719/19dewinead.htm Nation & World: DeWine blunder adds fuel to controversial September 11 ad - U.S. News & World Report<!-- Bot generated title -->] {{webarchive | url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081012183114/http://www.usnews.com/usnews/news/articles/060719/19dewinead.htm | date=October 12, 2008}}</ref><ref name="autogenerated2">{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2006/07/19/AR2006071901663.html|title=Washington Post}}{{dead link|date=June 2021|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> DeWine's campaign admitted that the video was actually a still photo of the World Trade Center with smoke digitally added.<ref name=autogenerated1 /> He was also criticized for using an emotionally charged image to attack his challenger.<ref name=autogenerated2 />

Another of DeWine's ads suggested that opponent Sherrod Brown did not pay his taxes for thirteen years. This claim led to the Associated Press reporting on October 19 that "Several Ohio television stations have stopped airing a Republican ad because state documents contradict the ad's accusation that Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Sherrod Brown didn't pay an unemployment tax bill for 13 years." Brown produced a commercial citing these facts.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://sherrodbrown.com/pages/dishonest | title=Sherrod Brown | access-date=March 14, 2010 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080306133718/http://sherrodbrown.com/pages/dishonest | archive-date=March 6, 2008}}</ref> DeWine's ads were changed to state only that he had failed to pay his unemployment taxes until legal action was taken against him.

On October 16, 2006, ''[[The New York Times]]'' reported that top national Republicans were moving resources away from the Ohio Senate race, as they had determined that DeWine was likely to lose, and wanted to spend money on races where Republican candidates were seen as having a better chance of winning.<ref>Adam Nagourney, [https://www.nytimes.com/2006/10/16/us/politics/16spend.html?_r=2&oref=slogin&pagewanted=print "In Final Weeks, G.O.P. Focuses on Best Bets"], ''The New York Times'', October 16, 2006.</ref>

=== Fundraising ===
During the election cycle, DeWine raised $14.9 million and spent $15.5 million.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.opensecrets.org/politicians/summary.php?cid=N00003709&cycle=2006 | title=Sen. Mike DeWine: Campaign Finance/Money - Summary - Senator 2006 {{!}} OpenSecrets | website=www.opensecrets.org|access-date=September 27, 2016}}</ref> Brown raised $8.9 million and spent $10.8 million.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.opensecrets.org/politicians/summary.php?cid=N00003535&cycle=2006 | title=Rep. Sherrod Brown: Campaign Finance/Money - Summary - Representative 2006 {{!}} OpenSecrets | website=www.opensecrets.org|access-date=September 27, 2016}}</ref>

=== Results ===
Brown was declared the winner right when the polls closed in [[Ohio]] at 7:30. DeWine had the second worst performance of a Republican incumbent in 2006; only Pennsylvania Senator [[Rick Santorum]] had a [[2006 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania|worse performance]]. While DeWine was able to win rural counties in western Ohio, Brown managed to win most eastern Ohio counties, especially in heavily populated areas. DeWine's narrow 2,000 vote victory in [[Hamilton County, Ohio|Hamilton County]], which is home to [[Cincinnati]], did not come close to making a dent in Brown's lead.

Brown would be reelected to a second term in [[2012 United States Senate election in Ohio|2012]], and a third term in [[2018 United States Senate election in Ohio|2018]]. Also in 2018, both Brown and DeWine were on the ballot, but this time for different races; DeWine would be [[2018 Ohio gubernatorial election|elected]] governor of Ohio. In 2024, Brown would be defeated for reelection.
